Optically Active 2,3-Allenoates via Palladium-Catalyzed
Carbonylation of Enantioenriched Propargylic Mesylates
Yuli Wanga and Shengming Ma a,b,*
a Shanghai Key Laboratory of Green Chemistry and Chemical Process, Department of Chemistry, East China Normal
University, 3663 North Zhongshan Lu, Shanghai 200062, People/C29s Republic of China
Fax : (+ 86) 21-62609305; e-mail: masm@sioc.ac.cn
b State Key Laboratory of Organometallic Chemistry, Shanghai Institute of Organic Chemistry, Chinese Academy of
Sciences, 345 Lingling Lu, Shanghai 200032, People/C29s Republic of China
Received: October 11, 2012; Revised: December 1, 2012; Published online: February 22, 2013
Supporting information for this article is available on the WWW under http://dx.doi.org/10.1002/adsc.201200910.
Abstract: Under mild conditions, optically active 2,3-
allenoates were synthesized from enantioenriched
propargylic mesylates with moderate to excellent
yields and high efficiency of chirality transfer by
using palladium(0) bis(dibenzylideneacetone)
(3 mol%) with ( S)-(/C0)-5,5’-bis(diphenylphosphino)-
4,4’-bi-1,3-benzodioxole [( S)-SEGPHOS] (3 mol%)
as the catalyst and diammonium hydrogen phosphate
(1.1 equiv.) as the base.
Keywords: carbonylation; chirality transfer; optically
active allenoates; palladium; propargylic mesylates
Introduction
2,3-Allenoates are a class of interesting and versatile
synthetic intermediates, which may undergo many re-
actions,
[1] such as nucleophilic addition reactions, [2]
electrophilic addition reactions, [1f, 3] Morita–Baylis–
Hillman reactions, [4] rearrangements,[5] cycloaddition[6]
and cyclization reactions, [1c,7] etc.[8] Many methods
have been reported for the synthesis of allenoates, [9]
but the preparation of optically active 2,3-allenoates
is not very well established (Scheme 1).
[10–18] Use of
stoichiometric chiral reagents and/or limited substrate
scopes are their main drawbacks.
Central-to-axial chirality transfer has been proven
to be an efficient strategy for the synthesis of optically
active allenes. In this field, Marshall et al. reported
the synthesis of chiral allenoates by using enantioen-
riched propargylic mesylates, which is very practical
for the terminal propargylic mesylates. However, seri-
ous racemization was observed for internal propargyl-
ic mesylates (Scheme 2).
[17]
Herein, we report a palladium-catalyzed carbonyla-
tion of enantioenriched non-terminal propargylic me-
sylates for the preparation of optically active 2,4-dis-
ubstituted 2,3-allenoates using Pd ACHTUNGTRENNUNG(dba)2 and ( S)-SEG-
PHOS as the catalyst.
Results and Discussion
We tried the reaction of enantioenriched ( S)-1-ethyl-
2-heptynyl methanesulfonate [( S)-1a]. Unfortunately,
the efficiency of chirality transfer was rather low
when PPh
3 was used as the ligand (Table 1, entry 1).
Then several optically active phosphorus ligands were
examined with the purpose to prevent racemization.
(S)-SEGPHOS provided the best results: the optical
purity of the product dropped to 96% from the enan-
tioenriched starting material with 99% ee, and the
yield was 70% (Table 1, entries 2–5). When ( R)-SEG-
PHOS was used, the efficiency of chirality transfer
dropped slightly, however, the reaction was very slow
(Table 1, entry 6). It is obvious that ( S)-SEGPHOS
matches the substrate ( S)-1a, while the R isomer does
not. Pd ACHTUNGTRENNUNG(acac)
2 also works with a lower yield (Table 1,
entry 7). Meanwhile, [PdCl ACHTUNGTRENNUNG(p-allyl)]2 is much less ef-
fective (Table 1, entry 8).
Solvent screening indicated that an ether is the
type of better solvent: Methyl tert-butyl ether gave
the best result (see the Supporting Information for
details on solvent effects). Several bases were also
tested in order to improve the yield and efficiency of
chirality transfer. Most of the bases, such as TEA,
pyridine, DIPEA and NaHCO
3 failed to improve the
yields with different stereoselectivity (Table 2, en-
tries 1–4); interestingly, when (NH
4)2HPO4 was used,
the yield was improved obviously, and the ee value of

Under our standard conditions, propargylic carbon-
ate could not form 2,3-allenoate; propargylic phos-

in moderate yield, but the enantiopurity of the prod-

many alcohols, and all the different allenoates were
obtained in good yields with very different ees: When
methanol was used, the ee value of the product was
80%; the enantiopurity dropped sharply in the pres-
ence of ethanol (84%); isobutyl alcohol performed
better with 90% ee (Scheme 3). In conclusion,

group. When R 2 is the smaller methyl group, the

tert-butyl and isopentyl, 2,3-allenoates could be pre-
pared in good yields with higher ee (94% ~ 97%)
(Table 3, entries 3–7), although the substrate with an
isopentyl group a required longer reaction time; in-
troducing a chlorine atom into the aliphatic alkyl
group has a very limited impact on the reaction
(Table 3, entry 8); when unsaturated groups, such as
phenyl and allyl groups, were introduced into R
2, the
efficiency of chirality transfer dropped slightly
(Table 3, entries 9 and 10); when R
2 is the 2-methyl-
allyl group, the corresponding 2,3-allenoate ( Ra)-2k
was obtained with 95% ee (Table 3, entry 11). Differ-
ent R 1 groups were also screened. With a longer
chain, the enantiopurity of the product dropped
slightly (Table 3, entry 12). The more sterically hin-
dered substrates ( S)-1m and ( S)-1n required longer
reaction times, but chirality transfer proceeded
smoothly (Table 3, entries 13 and 14). An allyl group
can also be introduced to R

Conclusions
In conclusion, we have developed an efficient method
for the synthesis of optically active 2,3-allenoates
from the readily available enantioenriched secondary
propargylic mesylates with moderate to excellent
yields and good stereoselectivities under very mild re-
action conditions by using the palladium catalysis and
(S)-SEGPHOS as the ligand: V arious alkyl, allyl, or
benzyl substituents may be successfully introduced
into the substrates. Further research in this area is
being pursued in our laboratory.
Experimental Section
General Information
NMR spectra were taken with a Bruker-300 spectrometer
(300 MHz for 1H NMR, 75.4 MHz for 13C NMR) or Bruker-
400 spectrometer (400 MHz for 1H NMR, 100.5 MHz for
13C NMR) in CDCl 3. Chemical shifts were recorded in ppm
relative to the residue of CHCl 3 in CDCl 3 and coupling con-
stants were reported in Hz. X-ray intensity data were mea-
sured at 293 K on a Bruker SMART APEX CCD-based X-
ray diffractometer system equipped with a fine-focus Mo-
target X-ray tube ( l = 0.71073 /C138) operated at 1,500 W . All
reactions were carried out in oven-dried tubes.
(NH
4)2HPO4was purchased from Sinopharm Chemical Re-
agent Co., Ltd; ( S)-SEGPHOS was purchased from Stream
Chemicals. MTBE was dried over sodium wire with benzo-
phenone as indicator and distilled freshly before use. The
enantioenriched propargylic mesylates were synthesized
from the corresponding enantiopure propargylic alcohols,
and used without further purification. Purification by
column chromatography was performed using Haiyang
(Shandong, China) silica gel (10–40 mL).
